lt:L2.02:0.text: A little cat named Pip was very **curious**. Every single day, Pip wanted to know what was happening on the other side of the garden wall.

lt:L2.02:1.text: One afternoon, Pip's curious nose led her straight into a bush, where she found a family of hedgehogs curled up asleep! Pip was so curious that she gently poked one with her paw.

lt:L2.02:2.text: The hedgehog woke up, uncurled, and gave a tiny, surprised squeak. Pip jumped back, but she was still curious — she sat and watched the hedgehogs for the rest of the afternoon, learning something new about her garden.

lt:L2.03:0.text: Grandpa was usually calm, but one afternoon he got absolutely **furious**. His favorite garden tools had gone missing from the shed, and he was sure someone had taken them without asking.

lt:L2.03:1.text: He searched the whole yard, muttering to himself, getting more and more furious with every empty corner. Then his granddaughter walked out holding the tools.

lt:L2.03:2.text: "I borrowed them to fix my bike, Grandpa — I forgot to tell you!" she said. Grandpa's furious face softened into a small smile.

lt:L2.03:3.text: "Next time," he said, "just tell me first, and I won't have to get furious over nothing."

lt:L2.04:0.text: Little Ana loved puzzles more than anything, but one rainy afternoon she found herself completely **puzzled**. Her grandmother had given her a box with no picture on the lid and no instructions inside — just three hundred loose pieces.

lt:L2.04:1.text: Ana sat there, puzzled, turning pieces over in her hands, unsure where to even begin. She tried the edges first, but she was still puzzled about which piece connected to which.

lt:L2.04:2.text: Finally, her grandmother sat beside her and said, "When you are puzzled, start with the corners — there are only four, and they always fit first." Ana found a corner, then another, and slowly her puzzled frown turned into a grin.

lt:L2.05:0.text: After a full day at the farm, feeding the animals, mending fences, and carrying heavy buckets of water, farmer Iqbal was completely **exhausted**. His arms ached, his legs felt like stone, and he could barely climb the steps to his own porch.

lt:L2.05:1.text: His son offered to finish the last chore, but Iqbal was too exhausted even to explain what needed doing — he just pointed and nodded. He sat down, closed his eyes, and within minutes he was fast asleep in his chair, still wearing his muddy boots.

lt:L2.05:2.text: When he woke an hour later, he felt much better, though still a little exhausted, and very glad his son had taken care of the rest.

lt:L2.06:0.text: Before crossing the busy market road, Aunt Rukhsana was always very **cautious**. She would stop at the edge, look left, then right, then left again, even if the road looked completely empty.

lt:L2.06:1.text: Her nephew used to tease her about being so cautious, saying it took forever just to cross one small street. One evening, though, a bicycle came speeding around the corner at exactly the moment they stepped off the curb — and because Aunt Rukhsana had been cautious and was watching closely, she pulled her nephew back just in time.

lt:L2.06:2.text: After that, her nephew never teased her again. "Better cautious than sorry," she always says, and now he says it too.

lt:L2.07:0.text: When the school bake sale raised more money than anyone expected, the head teacher decided to give every extra rupee to the small clinic down the road. She was **grateful** — truly grateful — for how hard the students had worked, baking and selling from early morning until the last plate was empty.

lt:L2.07:1.text: One student asked why she looked close to tears. "I am just so grateful," she said.

lt:L2.07:2.text: "You worked all day, and now families who could not afford medicine will get help." The students felt proud too, and decided that being the reason someone else got help was better than any prize. They planned an even bigger, more grateful bake sale for next year.

lt:L2.08:0.text: A young dog named Bruno was usually eager to try anything new, but the first time his owner brought out a bicycle, Bruno was strangely **reluctant**. He backed away, tail low, refusing to go anywhere near the strange spinning wheels.

lt:L2.08:1.text: His owner tried treats, gentle words, even a favorite toy — but Bruno stayed reluctant, watching from a safe distance. Then one afternoon, the owner simply sat beside the bicycle and let Bruno sniff it in his own time, with no pushing at all.

lt:L2.08:2.text: Slowly, Bruno's reluctant ears perked up, and he stepped closer. By the end of the week, the once-reluctant Bruno was trotting happily alongside the bicycle on every walk.

lt:L2.09:0.text: When the class hamster went missing from its cage on a Friday afternoon, every student was **delighted** to hear it had been found safe behind the bookshelf on Monday morning. The teacher was delighted too, and let the whole class take turns holding it gently, one by one.

lt:L2.09:1.text: One boy, who had been especially worried all weekend, was so delighted that he asked if he could bring the hamster home just for one night, to make sure it was really okay. His teacher smiled at how delighted — and relieved — he looked, and said yes, as long as his parents agreed.

lt:L2.09:2.text: That evening, the whole family took turns being delighted by the tiny hamster running on its wheel.

lt:L2.10:0.text: Uncle Hamid had asked his nephew, Bilal, to water the plants every single day while he was away — just that one job. When Hamid came home a week later and found every plant wilted and brown, he was **stubborn** about not letting it go.

lt:L2.10:1.text: "It's just water, once a day," he said, again and again, refusing to accept Bilal's excuses about being busy with exams. Bilal, just as stubborn, insisted exams mattered more than plants.

lt:L2.10:2.text: Neither would budge for two whole days. Finally, Hamid's wife stepped in and pointed out that both of them were being equally stubborn over something they could fix together in ten minutes.

lt:L2.10:3.text: They laughed, apologized, and replanted the garden side by side that weekend.

lt:L2.11:0.text: The night before her first big exam, Ayesha felt more **anxious** than she had ever felt before. Her stomach fluttered, her hands felt cold, and she kept checking the clock, worried she was somehow forgetting something important.

lt:L2.11:1.text: Her older sister noticed how anxious she looked and sat down beside her. "Being a little anxious means you care," her sister said, "but let's make a short plan so the anxious feeling has less to hold onto." Together they wrote down exactly what Ayesha needed for the morning, checked it twice, and set two alarms.

lt:L2.11:2.text: Ayesha still felt a bit anxious as she fell asleep, but far less than before — and in the morning, she walked into the exam room calm and ready.

lt:L2.12:0.text: A wealthy trader in the old bazaar was known across the whole street for being unusually **generous**. Every evening, before he closed his stall, he would give away whatever fruit and bread had not sold that day — never selling it cheap at the last minute, always simply giving it to whoever needed it most.

lt:L2.12:1.text: His neighbors thought he must be losing money, but the trader just smiled and said being generous had brought him more good luck and more loyal customers than any clever deal ever had. One winter, when his own stall caught fire, every single family he had once helped showed up the next morning with tools, wood, and cash to help him rebuild — proof, he said, that generous kindness always finds its way back.

lt:L2.13:0.text: Retrieval passage: A stubborn old goat named Bella refused to leave the muddy field even when it started to rain hard. Her owner, cautious as always, did not want to drag a furious, wet goat across a slippery yard, so he waited, patient, under the barn roof.

lt:L2.13:1.text: After an hour of stubborn standing in the rain, Bella finally got cold enough to trot inside on her own — no longer stubborn, just cautious about getting even wetter. Her owner laughed, dried her off, and said a stubborn goat always changes its mind eventually, as long as you stay cautious and let it happen in its own time.

lt:L3.02:0.text: Before bikes had rubber tires, riders used wheels with iron rims. Every bump in the road shook the whole bike — people called it a 'bone-shaker.' A ride that should have felt smooth instead felt rough and tiring.
